# Homework — Telling a Story with ggplot

### How to turn it in

Run your code in an R script and paste your **code, both plots (before and after), and your written answers** into a Word document to submit.

::: callout-tip
## Loading the data

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

tree_df <- read_excel("data/2026_06_25_tree_experiment_raw_data.xlsx")
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Task 1 — Write the sentence first (2 pts)

Pick `height_cm` or `width_cm`. Before writing any code, write the one-sentence finding you expect your final figure to show.

### Task 2 — Build a deliberately bad plot (2 pts)

Build a "busy" version of a comparison plot for your chosen variable: include at least one redundant element (an unnecessary facet or legend), the default alphabetical order, ggplot's default colors, and a title that is just the variable name. Show this plot.

### Task 3 — Redesign it (4 pts)

Fix it one step at a time, and briefly say what each fix improved:

a. Remove redundancy\
b. Order the groups with intent using `fct_relevel()`\
c. Choose a colorblind-safe palette with `scale_fill_manual()`\
d. Write a title that states the finding, with an appropriate subtitle and caption

### Task 4 — Annotate the one thing that matters (1 pt)

Add a single `annotate()` call that points at the specific number or region that supports your finding.

### Task 5 — The five-second test (1 pt)

Show your final figure to someone outside this class for five seconds, then hide it. Write down exactly what they said it showed, and whether it matched your Task 1 sentence.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Grading notes *(instructor — remove before posting)*

10 pts total. T1 finding sentence (2) · T2 deliberately bad plot with all 4 flaws present (2) · T3 four fixes each briefly explained (4) · T4 annotate() correctly placed (1) · T5 five-second test documented honestly, including a mismatch if one occurred (1). Watch for students who write a vague Task 1 sentence like "this shows the data" — push them to name the direction and the variables before they see Task 5's marking guidance.

*End of this homework.*
